content: Why does the picture made by a lens come out upside down on a wall? I thought the lens simply shrank the view and laid it on the wall, so turning it over seems like an extra thing the glass somehow does.

The lens does not flip a finished picture. Light from each point spreads out, and the lens bends those rays so they meet again. Rays from the top of the object cross the central region and meet near the bottom of the image; rays from the bottom meet near the top. That crossing creates the inversion naturally.
What makes those lines of light cross instead of just getting squeezed closer together? Is there one crossing place for the whole object, or does every little part have its own meeting spot?

Every small object point has its own matching image point. The curved surfaces change a ray's direction by different amounts depending on where it enters. For one object point, those differently bent rays converge at one location. The collection of many such locations forms the picture, so there is no single crossing point shared by the entire object.
If I slide the object closer, I assume the glass gets a shorter focal length because the crossing moves. Is focal length just the distance from the lens to wherever the sharp picture happens to land?

For a fixed lens in the same surrounding material, its focal length stays essentially fixed. What changes is the image distance. Focal length is defined using incoming rays that are parallel, as from a very distant object. For nearer objects, the rays arrive already spreading, so the lens needs more distance after bending them before they meet.
Then why does the image disappear from the wall when the object gets very close? The light is still crossing somewhere, so I would expect moving the wall far enough back to find it again.

Once the object is closer than one focal length, the rays leave the lens still spreading rather than converging. Your eyes can trace them backward to an apparent point, producing an upright virtual image, but no wall can catch that apparent meeting. Moving the wall cannot help because the rays never physically reunite on that side.

What decides how much larger a lens makes something look? It seems obvious that a wider piece of glass must give more magnification, because it has more bending area and can spread the picture across more space.

Width mainly controls how much light the lens collects, not how large the image is. Magnification is set by the object's position, the image's position, and the lens's focal length. A wider lens of the same shape and material usually gives the same image size, but it can make that image brighter by admitting more rays.
Why does moving the object matter if the lens bends every ray by the same amount? I can see how the picture would move forward or backward, but not why its height should change too.

The lens does not turn every ray through one fixed angle. Its effect depends on the ray's incoming direction and where it crosses the curved surface. When the object moves, the bundle reaching the lens has a different spread. The new geometry changes both where corresponding rays meet and the height of those meeting points.
Suppose I keep the object still and replace the lens with a bigger circle cut from the same kind of curve. Would the picture stay exactly the same size while only becoming brighter?

Ideally, yes: if the curvature, material, and thickness pattern are unchanged, enlarging the clear opening does not change focal length or magnification. It admits additional outer rays, increasing brightness. Real lenses can show more blur near their edges, so opening the full diameter may also reveal aberrations that a smaller opening hides.
Is that why a small hole can make a picture look sharper even though it looks dimmer? I had assumed sharpness and magnification were basically the same improvement, just described in different ways.

They are separate properties. Magnification describes image size relative to object size. Sharpness describes how tightly light from one object point is confined in the image. A smaller opening blocks troublesome outer rays and increases depth of field, often improving apparent sharpness, but it does not provide extra magnification and eventually diffraction adds blur.
Then what everyday change would actually increase the magnification without swapping the lens? Do I move the object toward the focus mark and chase the sharp image with the wall?

For a converging lens making a real image, move the object closer to the focal point while keeping it just outside that distance, then move the wall farther away to regain focus. The resulting image grows. This changes the object and image distances, while the lens's own focal length remains unchanged.

Why can a magnifying glass show an upright enlarged word when a lens projecting onto paper makes an upside-down picture? I thought enlargement came from using a larger lens, so the different direction is confusing.

The difference comes from where the object sits relative to the focal length, not from the lens diameter. Outside one focal length, outgoing rays can meet and form an inverted real image. Inside one focal length, they remain spread out; your eye traces them backward and sees an upright, enlarged virtual image on the object's side.
What does tracing backward mean here? The letters seem to be sitting behind the glass, and I am actually seeing them, so calling their location only apparent sounds like the light is somehow false.

The light is completely real; only its apparent source is different from its physical path. Your visual system usually assumes rays reaching the eye traveled in straight lines. After the lens bends spreading rays toward your eye, extending their final paths backward makes them seem to originate from a larger, more distant word.
Could I put a sheet where that larger word seems to be and get the same view printed on it? If not, what exactly prevents the sheet from catching the apparent picture?

No. At that apparent location, the outgoing rays are not actually passing through the corresponding image points; only backward extensions of their paths intersect there. A sheet records light that physically arrives at each spot. Since the rays are diverging, no placement on that side assembles them into the enlarged pattern your eye infers.
So if I move the word just beyond the special focus distance, what should I notice first: the upright view turning over, the image becoming smaller, or the place where it looks located changing?

Near the focal point, the apparent image moves extremely far away and the emerging rays approach parallel. Just beyond the focal distance, a real inverted image forms very far on the other side. As you move the word farther from the lens, that real image comes closer and generally becomes smaller. The transition is not a simple flip at one visible plane.

If a lens makes a blurry patch on a wall, why does sliding the wall sometimes make a detailed picture appear? I am fairly sure moving the wall changes the lens's focal length by giving the light a new stopping place.

Sliding the wall does not alter the lens's focal length. For a fixed object position, the lens sends rays from each object point toward a particular image plane. At that plane they form tight spots; before or after it, each bundle is still converging or has begun spreading, so neighboring spots overlap and look blurry.
What is the wall doing at the sharp position besides stopping the rays? Does the picture already exist in the air there, or does the paper somehow organize the light when it arrives?

The ray pattern exists at that plane before the wall is added. The wall mainly scatters the arriving light in many directions so your eyes can view it. It does not organize the image. Dust or mist can reveal parts of beams in the air, but placing a screen at the image plane makes the full pattern easy to see.
Why is there only one good wall position for one object distance? A thick object has a front and back, so I would think different parts demand different wall positions at the same time.

That is correct for a three-dimensional object. Points at different distances have slightly different best image distances. A single flat screen can coincide perfectly with only one of those planes, though nearby planes may look acceptably sharp. The range that appears sharp is called depth of field, and a smaller lens opening usually enlarges it.
If I move the object farther away while leaving the wall fixed, which way should I move the lens to recover the picture? I keep guessing the same direction as the object, but I cannot picture why.

As an object moves farther from a converging lens, its sharp real image moves closer to the lens, approaching one focal length away. With the wall fixed, you therefore move the lens so the required image distance matches the lens-to-wall gap. The exact direction in the room depends on which item you hold fixed, so distances are safer than a memorized direction.
What happens if the wall is tilted rather than straight across from the lens? Would one edge focus because it is closer while the other edge stays smeared, or can the lens tilt the picture too?

With the object and lens kept parallel, a tilted wall cuts through the image plane at an angle, so typically only a strip is sharply focused. Tilting the lens changes the geometry and can tilt the plane of sharp focus, a principle used in view cameras. It also introduces distortions, so alignment matters as well as distance.
Would making the glass wider solve that tilted-wall blur by covering more possible meeting places? My picture is that a bigger lens creates a larger focus zone, even if the distances stay unchanged.

A wider opening usually does the opposite: it makes defocus more noticeable because rays arrive over a broader range of angles. It gathers more light but narrows the range of positions that look acceptably sharp. Reducing the opening can hide some tilted-screen blur, though it cannot make a genuinely tilted plane coincide with a parallel image plane.

What happens to all the different light lines leaving one point when they enter a lens? I picture the glass giving every line the same inward turn, with the lens size deciding how enlarged the final picture becomes.

A lens changes each ray according to the angle at which it meets each surface. Rays entering near different parts therefore receive different direction changes, arranged so they converge approximately at one image point. The lens diameter decides how many of those rays are accepted; image magnification comes from the object and image geometry instead.
Why do ray drawings usually show only three neat lines, then? If light leaves the point in every direction, those few lines seem too special to explain the whole bright patch.

Those are convenient construction rays, not the only rays present. One parallel to the axis refracts through the far focal point, one through the optical center is approximately undeviated, and one aimed through the near focal point emerges parallel. Their intersection locates the image point; all other admitted rays should converge there too in an ideal lens.
Is the line through the middle truly unbent, or is that another drawing shortcut? The glass still has two surfaces there, so it seems odd that this particular light line gets a free pass.

It is a thin-lens approximation. Near the optical center, the two surfaces are locally close to parallel, so the ray bends at both boundaries but emerges nearly parallel to its original direction, with only a small sideways shift. Thick lenses require more careful reference planes, and an off-axis central ray may not behave so simply.
Then why does blocking most of the lens not remove most of the picture? I would expect each patch of glass to carry one matching patch of the object, like pieces of a window view.

Every small region of the lens receives rays from nearly every visible object point. Blocking part of the lens removes some rays from every image point, so the whole picture remains but becomes dimmer. It may also become sharper by losing aberrant outer rays. A patch maps ray direction, not a matching tile of the finished image.
What is special about the focus mark of a lens? I have been treating it as the place where any object makes a sharp picture, and I assume it shifts closer to the glass when I move the object closer.

The focal point is where rays arriving parallel to the axis meet after a converging lens. Those rays correspond approximately to an object extremely far away. A nearby object sends spreading rays, so its image forms beyond the focal point. Moving that object changes the image location, while the focal length of the unchanged lens stays fixed.
Why do the rays come out parallel when the object itself sits on the focus mark? They started by spreading from one spot, so I do not see how parallel lines can still contain a picture.

For one object point on the focal plane, the lens converts its spreading bundle into a parallel bundle traveling in a particular direction. Different points across the object produce parallel bundles with different directions. The image information is therefore carried in angle rather than gathered into a finite image plane; another lens can convert those directions back into positions.
Could an extremely distant wall catch that picture, since parallel lines must eventually reach it? Or does the picture count as being infinitely far away even though every ray hits some real surface?

A distant wall receives the rays, but each parallel bundle stays broad instead of converging to one corresponding point. Bundles from different object points overlap, so the wall does not show a focused picture. Saying the image is at infinity is shorthand for the outgoing bundles being parallel and requiring infinite distance to converge under the simple geometric model.
If I place a second lens in those parallel lines, what decides where the picture returns? I would guess the first lens's new focal length still controls the landing place after I moved the object.

The first lens has not acquired a new focal length. It prepares bundles whose directions encode object position. The second lens brings each parallel bundle to a point in its own focal plane, so that second focal length largely sets the final image scale and location. This is the basic geometry behind telescopes and some relay systems.

Does that mean sliding the second lens along a perfectly parallel bundle should not change where the picture sits relative to that lens? That sounds different from focusing a single lens on a nearby object.

Yes, in the ideal parallel region, sliding the second lens leaves the final image one focal length behind that lens, so the image moves along with it. A nearby object does not supply parallel bundles, and changing the lens position then changes both object distance and required image distance. Real beams have finite width and alignment limits.

Why does a lens that caves inward make things look smaller instead of forming a little picture on the other side? I thought choosing a sufficiently large piece would eventually give enough magnification to project it.

An inward-curving, or diverging, lens spreads parallel rays rather than bringing them together. Its diameter can collect more rays, but it does not reverse that spreading action. For a normal real object by itself, the outgoing rays appear to come from a smaller upright virtual image on the object's side, so no screen on the far side catches it.
What is a negative focus supposed to mean? A distance cannot really be less than nothing, so I imagine it is just a label for a weak lens rather than an actual place.

The negative sign records direction, not a physically negative length. After a diverging lens, parallel rays spread as though they originated from a point on the incoming side. Extending the outgoing rays backward locates that focal point. Under the usual sign convention, its side makes the focal length negative; strength is described by the magnitude.
Can that spreading lens ever help make a real picture, or is it only useful for shrinking what the eye sees? I have seen paired lenses but cannot tell which one does the actual picture-making.

It can help within a combination. A converging lens may first create a bundle that is already heading toward a meeting point; a diverging lens can weaken that convergence, moving the final image farther away or changing its size. In a multi-lens system, image formation belongs to the sequence, not exclusively to one piece.
If I hold the two lenses together, do their powers simply cancel when their curves look equally strong? The thicknesses look similar, so I would expect no bending and no image change.

They cancel only if their optical powers are equal and opposite. Power depends on surface curvatures, refractive index, thickness, and surrounding material, so appearance alone is unreliable. For thin lenses touching each other, powers approximately add. A zero sum makes the pair afocal, but rays can still shift or show imperfections in real elements.

If a wider lens gathers more light, why does opening a camera lens make the background blurrier? Bigger glass should make everything larger and therefore easier to see clearly, since magnification only comes from lens size.

Opening the aperture uses a wider portion of the lens, but it does not by itself enlarge the image. It admits rays over a broader range of angles. At the exact image plane those rays meet, while slightly nearer or farther planes produce larger blur circles. Consequently, a wide opening gives more light but less depth of field.
What is a blur circle in ordinary terms? I picture an unfocused point turning into a fuzzy dot, but I do not know why the dot's width follows the opening rather than the glass curve.

Imagine a cone of rays narrowing toward its correct image point and widening after it. A sensor placed away from the cone's tip cuts it as a small disk rather than a point. A wider aperture makes the cone broader and steeper, so the same focusing error produces a larger disk. Curvature still determines where the tip belongs.
Why can the main subject stay the same size when the opening changes? If extra edge rays join the picture, I would expect them to extend its borders instead of piling onto the same points.

Edge rays from a given object point are directed toward the same corresponding image point as central rays. They add brightness at that point rather than creating more distant image points. The picture's borders come from which object points are included and the system's magnification, while the aperture controls how many paths from each point get through.
Does closing the opening always keep adding sharpness, then? A tiny gap seems as if it should select one perfect line from every point and remove nearly all the ways light can miss.

Only up to a point. Closing the aperture reduces defocus and many lens aberrations, but a very small opening makes light spread by diffraction. The image then softens even at perfect focus. Practical systems balance aberration, diffraction, brightness, and desired depth of field rather than treating the smallest opening as automatically best.
If the object moves closer while the opening stays fixed, does the focal length shorten to keep the cone tip near the sensor? Cameras seem to adjust something without moving very far.

Ordinary focusing usually changes the spacing between lens elements and the sensor, or moves internal elements, so the required image plane lands on the sensor. A simple fixed lens retains its focal length when the object moves. Some internal-focus designs do change effective focal length slightly, but that is a consequence of rearranging the optical system.
Then what does the number written as an f-stop compare? Is it measuring the clear hole, the focal length, or some combined amount that predicts both brightness and background blur?

An f-number is the focal length divided by the effective aperture diameter. A lower number means a wider relative opening, generally admitting more light and reducing depth of field for the same framing conditions. Because it is a ratio, the same physical hole can represent different f-numbers on lenses with different focal lengths.

Why does the sharp picture move when I move the object, even though the lens stays put? I thought each object distance gives the lens a different focal length, but diagrams keep marking one fixed focus point.

The fixed mark is the lens's focal point for parallel incoming rays. A nearer object sends more strongly spreading rays, which need a longer distance after the lens to converge. A farther object sends less spreading rays, so they meet closer to the focal plane. Thus image distance changes while the lens's focal length remains fixed.
Is there a simple connection between the two distances, or is the new picture position something found only by drawing lines? I want to know why a small move near the focus causes such a large shift.

For a thin lens, the relationship is one over focal length equals one over object distance plus one over image distance. When the object distance is only slightly greater than the focal length, their reciprocal values are nearly equal, leaving a very small reciprocal for image distance. A small object shift can therefore imply a very large image shift.
What happens at the other extreme when the object is very far away? Does the image squeeze right onto the focus mark, and would it then become too small to have any recognizable detail?

As object distance becomes very large, the image plane approaches one focal length behind the lens. The image can be small, but detail is not automatically lost: its size depends on the object's angular extent and the focal length. The Moon is distant yet forms a finite image because it spans a noticeable angle in the sky.

If I exchange the wall and the glowing object without moving the lens, should the light rebuild the object at its old place? That sounds plausible, but ordinary objects do not send light as tidy points.

In ideal optics, light paths are reversible. If a patterned light source is placed in the former image plane, the lens forms its image in the former object plane, with the distance roles exchanged. An ordinary illuminated object is also a collection of points sending many rays, so tidiness is not required; enough rays merely need to enter the lens.

How can two lenses make a much larger distant view when neither piece looks especially wide? I assumed magnification only depends on glass size, so a narrow telescope should not be able to enlarge much.

A telescope's angular magnification mainly comes from the ratio of the objective's focal length to the eyepiece's focal length, not their widths. The objective forms an intermediate image of the distant scene. The eyepiece then lets your eye inspect that image under a larger angle. Diameter chiefly affects brightness and fine-detail resolution.
What is the middle picture between the lenses? Is it a real tiny scene that I could catch on paper, or is it only another apparent view meant for the second lens?

In a common astronomical telescope, the objective forms a real, inverted intermediate image near its focal plane. You can remove the eyepiece and place a small screen there to catch it. The eyepiece is positioned so that this intermediate image lies near its own focal plane, producing a comfortable magnified virtual view.
Why does a longer front lens and a shorter eye lens give more enlargement? The words longer and shorter refer to distances, but the result I see is an angle, which feels unrelated.

The objective turns a small incoming angle into a physical height at its focal plane; a longer objective focal length makes that height larger. The eyepiece converts that height back into an outgoing angle; a shorter eyepiece focal length makes the angle larger. Combining both conversions gives approximately their focal-length ratio.
If I separate the lenses more, does the front lens gain focal length because its picture has farther to travel? I would expect that to increase the enlargement without changing either piece of glass.

Separating them does not change either lens's focal length. A correctly adjusted telescope places the objective's image near the eyepiece's focal plane. Changing separation shifts that image relative to the eyepiece, mainly altering focus and whether outgoing rays are comfortable for the eye. It does not provide the straightforward magnification increase you expect.
What does the width of the front lens improve if not enlargement? A larger opening looks as though it should at least reveal smaller features rather than merely making the same blurred view brighter.

It improves both light collection and diffraction-limited resolution. A wider objective gathers more light from faint objects and allows finer angular details to remain distinct. The eyepiece can enlarge whatever detail the objective captured, but it cannot recover detail that a small objective blurred together. Width therefore matters greatly, just not as the main magnification control.
If I cover the left half of a lens, why does the right half of the picture not vanish? I thought a lens worked like a window, with each glass area carrying the matching area of the view.

Each point on the object sends rays toward many parts of the lens. Either half therefore receives information from the whole object and can form the whole image. Covering the left half removes roughly half the rays contributing to every image point, so the picture becomes dimmer rather than losing its right or left side.
What if I leave only a tiny clear corner instead of a full half? Would the entire scene still appear, and would it be shifted because the remaining light comes through off to one side?

The entire scene can still appear if that corner receives rays from all its points. In an ideal thin lens, those rays still head toward the same image locations, so the image is not substantially shifted. It becomes much dimmer, and diffraction or off-axis imperfections may soften or distort it.
Surely using the full lens must make the picture larger, because the outer light reaches farther across the wall. Why else would magnification depend on lens size at all?

Magnification does not ordinarily depend on the clear diameter. Outer rays from one object point travel at steeper angles but still converge on that point's assigned image location; they do not extend the picture's boundary. Diameter changes brightness, diffraction, and aberrations. Focal length and the object-image distances set the image's overall size.
Why might the uncovered corner produce a slightly worse shape if the ideal meeting points are unchanged? Is that because real glass has uneven bending away from the middle?

Partly. Real lenses do not bring every ray to exactly the ideal point, especially far from the optical axis or near the outer edge. Using an off-center patch samples asymmetric aberrations such as coma and astigmatism. Manufacturing errors can contribute too, but even a perfectly made spherical lens has predictable off-axis imperfections.

If I slide that tiny opening across the covered lens, could I compare the little views to test different areas? I am unsure whether each view should brighten the same places or reveal different errors.

Yes. Moving a small aperture across the lens selects different ray bundles while preserving the whole scene. Differences in image position, sharpness, or distortion reveal local slope errors and systematic aberrations; brightness may also vary because of coatings or blockage. This idea underlies several optical tests, although precise measurements need controlled point sources and geometry.
Does the same whole-picture rule explain why squinting can sharpen a blurry view? My eyelids leave only a narrow opening, yet I do not see merely a thin stripe of the scene.

Yes. The narrower opening blocks many rays from every scene point rather than selecting one stripe of the scene. Smaller ray bundles make defocus circles on the retina smaller, so the view can seem sharper. It also reduces light and introduces diffraction if extremely narrow, which is why squinting is a limited optical workaround.
What is the curved glass actually doing that flat glass cannot do? I think the middle is thicker simply to delay those rays more, and a bigger lens should delay more and magnify more.

The crucial effect is direction change at surfaces where the refractive index changes. Curvature gives different surface tilts at different heights, so rays are redirected by different amounts toward a common point. Extra travel time through the thicker middle is related to the wave description, but diameter alone does not set magnification.
Why does light change direction at the surface in the first place? Saying it slows down in glass seems incomplete, because a car slowing on a road does not automatically turn toward the middle.

The turning occurs when one side of a wavefront enters the slower material before the other side. That side advances more slowly while the other continues faster, rotating the wavefront and therefore the travel direction. If the whole wave enters straight on at once, it slows without turning. This relationship is summarized by Snell's law.
Does the second surface undo the first bend when light leaves the glass? The outside air is the original material again, so I would expect the ray to return to its starting direction.

It would return to its original direction if the second surface were parallel to the first, as in a flat window pane. In a lens, the two surface normals generally point in different directions. The second refraction therefore does not simply undo the first; together the two bends produce convergence or divergence.
If I put the same lens under water, would its focus move because the object appears closer, or because the glass itself bends less strongly when water surrounds it?

The lens itself becomes optically weaker because water's refractive index is closer to that of glass than air's is. Each boundary causes less direction change, so a converging glass lens generally gets a longer focal length in water. Apparent object position can also matter in a mixed setup, but the surrounding medium directly changes lens power.
Why can one lens picture be caught on a card while another can only be seen by looking through the glass? I assume the card version happens when the lens is physically larger and throws more light.

Catchability depends on whether rays physically converge, not mainly on lens diameter. A real image forms where rays from each object point actually meet, so a card can intercept the pattern. A virtual image forms where spreading rays only appear to originate when traced backward; your eye can interpret those directions, but a card cannot collect an apparent crossing.
What does my eye add that the card lacks? Both receive light at their surfaces, so it sounds as though the eye is making a second picture from the directions rather than catching the first one.

Exactly. Your eye contains another converging lens that takes the incoming directions and forms a real image on the retina. The brain interprets those directions as coming from locations in the scene. A plain card only scatters whatever intensity pattern reaches its surface; it has no lens to reorganize a diverging bundle into focused retinal points.
If I add a second lens before the card, can it turn any virtual picture into a real one? I am vague about where that second lens would need to sit.

Often it can. The first lens supplies rays with a particular spread, and the second lens can bend them into converging bundles if its power and position are suitable. For the second lens, the virtual image from the first system acts as an object described by the incoming ray directions. The required placement follows the lens equation.
Does moving the original object change the first lens's focal length when the picture switches from card-catchable to only apparent? The switch seems too sharp to come from distance alone.

The focal length stays fixed. The switch occurs as the object crosses the focal plane. Just outside it, outgoing rays converge very far away and make a real image. At it, they are parallel. Just inside it, they diverge and define a virtual image. A continuous change in ray angle produces the apparently sharp category change.
What would I observe exactly at that crossing point if I moved the object slowly? Would the card image grow without limit and become too dim before it disappears?

As the object approaches the focal plane from outside, the real image moves farther away and its geometric magnification increases. On any fixed card it goes out of focus, and a card moved to follow it receives light spread over a growing area, so it becomes dim. At the focal plane, no finite card position captures a focused image.
Why do simple lenses put colored outlines around a sharp-looking object? I thought every color followed the same route and lens width only controlled how large the shared picture became.

Glass bends different wavelengths by slightly different amounts, a property called dispersion. Blue light usually experiences a higher refractive index than red light, so a simple lens gives them different focal lengths. A screen at one plane cannot focus all colors perfectly, producing colored fringes. Lens diameter affects their visibility but not ordinary magnification.
What does a different focal length for each color mean when there is only one piece of glass? Is the focus mark really a stack of nearby colored places rather than a single point?

Yes, for a simple real lens the marked focus is an approximation, often specified for one reference wavelength. Parallel red, green, and blue rays can meet at slightly different axial positions. Each color also changes image size slightly away from the center, so chromatic blur may appear both along the axis and toward image edges.
Can closing the opening remove the colored edges, or does that only hide ordinary fuzziness? A smaller hole seems as though it would force all colors down the same central route.

Closing the aperture can reduce the visible blur because narrower ray bundles make smaller out-of-focus spots, especially for axial color error. It does not make the refractive indices equal or truly merge the focal lengths. Some sideways color scaling can remain. Very small apertures also add diffraction and reduce brightness.
Why do two joined lenses help if each one splits the colors? I would expect their mistakes to add, unless one piece somehow bends red more and blue less in reverse order.

That reverse balancing is the idea. Designers pair glasses with different dispersion and give one element positive power and another negative power. Their overall bending can remain converging while their color-dependent differences partly cancel. An achromatic doublet commonly brings two wavelengths to the same focus, though residual color remains across the full spectrum.
If I move the object, do those colored focal lengths move with it? I still tend to think the focal length follows the picture position whenever the subject distance changes.

The lens retains its wavelength-dependent focal lengths when the object moves. What moves are the red, green, and blue image planes associated with the new object distance. Their separations may change in practical terms, but that follows the imaging equation for each fixed color-specific focal length, not a focal length that tracks the object.
What causes the plain white blur near the edge even when I use only one color of light? Is that a separate failure of the curved shape rather than the color problem?

Yes. With one wavelength, spherical aberration can make outer and inner rays focus at different distances, while coma and astigmatism affect off-axis points asymmetrically. These arise from lens geometry rather than dispersion. Changing surface shapes, combining elements, or restricting the aperture can reduce them, but each remedy involves tradeoffs.
How does the eye keep a nearby page and a distant sign clear at different times? I assumed the eye lens changes focal length simply because the object moved, like any lens responding to distance.

An ordinary rigid lens does not respond to object distance, but the eye actively changes its lens shape. Muscles alter the curvature, changing optical power and therefore focal length so the image remains on the fixed retina. This active process is accommodation; it is not the object directly changing a passive lens.
Why can the retina not move forward and backward instead, as a wall does behind a glass lens? It seems mechanically simpler than squeezing the clear part into a new curve.

The retina lines the inside of the eyeball and is connected to delicate tissue, blood vessels, and nerves, so translating it would be mechanically difficult. Changing lens curvature provides a compact way to adjust optical power while image distance stays nearly fixed. Some animals use different focusing mechanisms, including moving a lens, but human eyes mainly accommodate by reshaping it.
Does the dark opening in front decide how large the retinal picture is? Since it gets wider in dim light, I thought it also magnified objects to compensate for seeing less detail.

The pupil mainly controls how much light enters and how broad the ray bundles are. Widening it does not substantially magnify the retinal image; eye geometry and optical power set that scale. A larger pupil helps brightness but reduces depth of field and can expose more aberrations, which may actually reduce sharpness in dim conditions.
What exactly changes when someone needs a distance lens in front of the eye? Is that extra glass moving the focus point back onto the retina without making the viewed object much larger?

Yes. Corrective lenses alter the vergence, meaning the convergence or divergence, of light before it enters the eye. They compensate when the eye's relaxed optical power or length would place the image in front of or behind the retina. They can cause some size change, especially with strong prescriptions, but refocusing is their main purpose.
